cards.text: We're in Jeremiah, friend, and the message just spent a long stretch on idols that can't even walk. Now it turns to the people of the land. These are people living under siege, with the enemy right outside their walls.

cards.question: The people living under siege get their first order. What are they told to do?

answers.text: Gather up their belongings from the land
Rebuild the walls around their city
Open the gates to the enemy army

cards.text: Pack your bags. Friend, when they slid me into that junk drawer, I didn't get to pack ONE thing! Then the LORD says why: He's going to sling the people of the land right out of it.

cards.question: The LORD says He'll sling the people out of the land someday, far off in the future.
The LORD says He'll bring distress on the people of the land so that they may be ___.

cards.text: Then the speaker cries out, and it gets personal: "Woe to me because of my brokenness; my wound is grievous!"

cards.question: Right after crying woe over that wound, what does the speaker say about it?

answers.text: It is my sickness and I must bear it
Someone else caused it and must fix it
It will heal on its own before long

cards.text: Now the picture is a tent. The speaker's tent is destroyed, and ALL its ropes are snapped. Not one rope, friend. ALL of them.

cards.question: With the tent destroyed, the speaker's sons are still close by, ready to help put it back up.
With the sons gone and the tent torn down, who's left to pitch it again and set up the curtains?

cards.text: So how did it get this bad? The speaker points at the shepherds: they've become senseless, and they do not seek the LORD. That's a tour guide who REFUSES to look at the map.

cards.question: Because the shepherds don't seek the LORD, they have not prospered, and all their ___ is scattered.

cards.text: Then, LISTEN! The sound of a report is coming, a great commotion, the kind of noise that makes you freeze in bed at 2 a.m.

cards.question: Where is this great commotion coming from?
When the commotion arrives, the cities of Judah will be left full and thriving.

cards.text: Judah's cities will be a desolation, a haunt for jackals. When the jackals move in, friend, that neighborhood is NOT on the way up.

cards.question: Talking straight to the LORD, the speaker admits that no one who walks directs his own steps.

cards.text: Then the speaker asks the LORD for correction. Me? I can't even take correction from an oven timer!

cards.question: How does the speaker ask the LORD to correct him?

answers.text: Only with justice and not in anger
Quickly so that it will soon be over
Gently and only where no one can see

cards.question: The speaker says that correction in the LORD's anger would bring him to ___.

cards.text: Then the prayer turns toward the nations that do not acknowledge the LORD, the families that do not call on His name.

cards.question: The speaker asks the LORD to pour out His ___ on the nations that do not acknowledge Him.
Why does the speaker ask the LORD to pour out wrath on those nations?

cards.text: The prayer calls God's people Jacob, after the man whose sons became the tribes of Israel. Those nations have consumed him, finished him off and devastated his homeland.

findings.problem: The opening card never says who is speaking. 'We're in Jeremiah' names the book, not the prophet. Jeremiah's first appearance should also say simply who he is, like 'Jeremiah, a prophet'.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: The card states a Bible fact from the passage before this one: idols that can't walk (Jeremiah 10:5). It gives no reference, and the card cites only Jeremiah 10:17.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: No story card sets up the turn from the jackals to the speaker praying to the LORD, so this true-or-false statement arrives with no context to reason from. 'Admits' also renames what the text says, which is 'I know'. 'Admits' implies a reluctance the text doesn't give.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.
Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The joke compares taking correction from the LORD to taking correction from an oven timer. An oven timer doesn't correct anyone, so the comparison doesn't share the core action, and it needs explaining to click.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The blank tests the wording 'bring me to nothing', not a meaning the baker can reason out. 'Tears' and 'shame' are equally believable results of being corrected in anger, so getting it right is luck.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card states a Bible fact from outside the passage: Jacob is the man whose sons became the tribes of Israel. It gives no reference for it, such as Genesis 35:22-26 or Genesis 49:28.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: From Jeremiah 10:19 on, the cards call the 'I' voice 'the speaker'. The text doesn't say whether it is Jeremiah or the land or people personified. papa-dorin.md asks him to say who is speaking before quoting an 'I', while the leave-open rule covers only who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.
findings.question: When the text leaves unclear who the 'I' is, as in Jeremiah 10:19-25, should Papa Dorin say 'the speaker', name Jeremiah, or say plainly that the voice could be Jeremiah or the people?
